title: Masorti worldwide
hook: Masorti communities in Israel, Europe and Latin America

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was egalitarian: the woman in the second row, and the voice at the door saying ten. Today, the same movement, far from where it began.

Friday evening in Buenos Aires. The street is loud, the synagogue is louder. Families crowd in, kids slide along the benches, someone is already humming the tune before the cantor starts. The prayers are in Hebrew, the same words said in Jerusalem and London tonight. But the rabbi's welcome is in Spanish, and so are the jokes during the announcements. Afterward, out on the sidewalk, people say Shabbat shalom and then switch to arguing about football. Nobody here calls their synagogue Conservative. They use another word, the one you met three days ago.
screen: `FRIDAY NIGHT, BUENOS AIRES.` → `HEBREW PRAYERS, SPANISH WELCOME.` → `NOT CONSERVATIVE. MASORTI.`

segments.voice: Masorti worldwide. Masorti is Hebrew for traditional, and outside North America it is the name this movement goes by. The approach is the one you've been learning: halakha as binding, and halakha that develops, with rabbis reasoning from the sources and congregations choosing among approved answers. Now take it on a short trip. First, Latin America. In Buenos Aires a rabbinical seminary trains rabbis to teach and lead in Spanish and Portuguese, so a community in South America can be led by someone who grew up in its own language. Second, Israel. There the official rabbinate is Orthodox, and Masorti congregations build their life alongside it: their own synagogues, schools and rabbis, often trained in Jerusalem. Keeping tradition in Hebrew, at home, while asking for a place in the public square. Third, Europe. In Britain and on the continent there are Masorti synagogues, some large, some small enough that everyone knows who brought the cake. Each one sounds like where it is: the accents differ, the tunes differ, the food after services differs. What travels is the method: take the law seriously, and let it develop. A psalm says it in one line: "O sing unto the LORD a new song: sing unto the LORD, all the earth." All the earth, in many accents.
screen: `MASORTI MEANS TRADITIONAL.` · `LATIN AMERICA: RABBIS IN SPANISH.` · `ISRAEL: ALONGSIDE AN ORTHODOX RABBINATE.` · `EUROPE: EACH SOUNDS LIKE WHERE IT IS.` · then, large: `SING UNTO THE LORD, ALL THE EARTH.`

segments.voice: Choose one of the three places: Buenos Aires, Jerusalem, or a small synagogue somewhere in Europe. Let it come into focus: the language on the street, a tune you might know in a new accent, the people lingering after the service. Hold that one community in mind and wish it well, in whatever way you wish people well.
Masorti worldwide. The name Conservative Judaism goes by outside North America: one approach to the law, lived in Hebrew, Spanish, Portuguese and many other languages. Today's word.
Your line: worldwide. One way of living the tradition, carried into many languages. Until tomorrow.
